issues.legal_issue: An acquittal may be reversed in an appeal when the reviewing court perversely rejects satisfactory incriminating evidence on grounds that do not undermine its value.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused on the evidence of an injured eyewitness and corroborating circumstances.

The High Court acquitted the accused after rejecting the eyewitness’s evidence and discounting corroborating evidence for reasons the Supreme Court found flimsy, irrelevant, or inconsistent with the record.
The eyewitness’s account was supported by evidence of his serious injuries, medical evidence, and other witnesses; the evidence, viewed as a whole, supported only the conclusion of guilt.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s acquittal was perverse. The Court set it aside and restored the convictions entered by the trial court.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court ordinarily does not interfere unless the acquittal is perverse. State of U.P. v. Gokaran holds that interference is warranted when satisfactory incriminating evidence is brushed aside on the basis of circumstances that do not detract from its value. The Court also relied on Allarakha K. Mansuri v. State of Gujarat for the principle that defective investigation by itself is not a ground for acquittal. The benefit-of-doubt principles referred to in Harijana Thirupala v. Public Prosecutor and Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh did not apply because the evidence was neither ambivalent nor reasonably consistent with innocence.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding challenged an appellate court’s acquittal of persons who had been convicted at trial.
predicates.satisfactory_incriminating_evidence_supp: The prosecution presented incriminating evidence, including an injured eyewitness’s account and corroborating evidence, that supported guilt.
predicates.acquittal_reasons_did_not_detract_from_e: The reviewing court rejected incriminating evidence for reasons that did not materially undermine its reliability or force.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and satisfactory evidence supports guilt, an acquittal based on reasons that do not undermine that evidence may be set aside and the convictions restored.

issues.legal_issue: An injured child eyewitness’s testimony is not rendered unreliable merely because the statement was recorded late or because an investigator did not obtain it in writing when the delay is explained and the evidence is credible.
material_facts: A child eyewitness suffered serious head and other injuries during the attack and was initially unable to speak coherently.
Medical personnel, the investigating officer, and several neighbours described the child as semi-conscious or unable to communicate after the attack.
The investigating officer tried to obtain the child’s statement while he was in hospital but recorded it only after learning that the child had been discharged and locating him elsewhere.
The eyewitness’s account was corroborated by medical evidence and other testimony.
The High Court relied on the delay and the failure to obtain a written statement to disbelieve the eyewitness.
issues.conclusion: The delay was adequately explained and did not justify rejecting the eyewitness’s testimony; the circumstances did not make it reasonable to expect the injured child to provide a written statement while incapacitated.
issues.legal_principle: Mohd. Khalid v. State of West Bengal holds that delay in examining a witness is not invariably fatal; when the delay is explained, the court may act on testimony found credible. Balakrushna Swain v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. Brahmahanda Nanda do not establish that delay by itself destroys credibility; unexplained delay may raise suspicion, and the court must assess the explanation. The Court also applied the principle in Allarakha K. Mansuri v. State of Gujarat that defective investigation alone does not warrant acquittal, and stressed that witness evidence must be assessed with an empathetic appreciation of the witness’s circumstances.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_injured_eyewitness and statement_recorded_after_delay and delay_explained_by_incapacity_and_investigative_efforts and testimony_credible_and_corroborated

predicates.criminal_case_with_injured_eyewitness: The proceeding involved criminal allegations and testimony from a person injured in the alleged offence.
predicates.statement_recorded_after_delay: The investigating officer recorded the injured eyewitness’s statement after a delay following the incident.
predicates.delay_explained_by_incapacity_and_invest: The eyewitness was initially unable to communicate because of injuries, and the investigator made efforts to obtain a statement before the eyewitness became available.
predicates.testimony_credible_and_corroborated: The injured eyewitness’s account was supported by medical evidence and other testimony.

issues.definition: When an injured eyewitness in a criminal case gives a credible, corroborated account after a delay explained by incapacity and investigative efforts, the account is not rejected merely because it was delayed or not obtained in writing.

issues.legal_issue: The death penalty is not justified when the circumstances of the offence do not make the case one of the rarest of rare cases.
material_facts: The trial court imposed the death penalty on the accused it regarded as the ringleader in a planned murder.
The Supreme Court maintained the convictions but found that the circumstances did not place the case among the rarest of rare cases.
issues.conclusion: The Court reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment and maintained the other sentences imposed on that accused.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rarest-of-rare standard for imposing the death penalty. It cited no earlier case for this sentencing determination.

predicates.death_sentence_under_review: The proceeding included review of a sentence of death imposed after conviction for a serious offence.
predicates.circumstances_not_rarest_of_rare: The circumstances of the offence did not make the case one of the rarest of rare cases.

issues.definition: When a death sentence is under review and the circumstances are not among the rarest of rare, the death sentence is replaced with life imprisonment.
